tip: Τι κάνεις (ti kanis) is literally 'what are you doing?' – it's the everyday 'how are you?'. The standard reply: καλά (kala = fine).
Γεια σου (ya su) is for one friend – with a group or a stranger it becomes γεια σας (ya sas).
Καλησπέρα (kalispera) takes over from late afternoon on – καλημέρα (kalimera) covers morning to early afternoon.
Καληνύχτα (kalinikhta) is only for parting at night – to greet someone in the evening, use καλησπέρα (kalispera).
The -ετε (-ete) ending is the polite form: τι κάνετε (ti kanete) with strangers and elders, τι κάνεις (ti kanis) with friends.
Χαίρετε (kherete) is a polite all-purpose hello – safe with strangers, officials, anyone whose formality level you can't guess.
Με λένε (me lene) is literally 'they call me' – the everyday way to say 'my name is' in Greek.
Πώς σε λένε; (pos se lene) is literally 'how do they call you?' – Greek asks names with 'they call', not 'what is your name'.
Σας λένε (sas lene) is the polite way to ask a name; with a friend it drops to σε λένε (se lene).
Ονομάζομαι (onomazome) is the slightly formal 'my name is' – everyday speech prefers με λένε (me lene).
Greek usually puts 'the' before names: η Σοφία (i Sofia), literally 'the Sofia'. Skipping the article sounds off.
Nationality words change with gender: a Greek woman is Ελληνίδα (Elinidha), a Greek man is Έλληνας (Elinas).
No 'you' needed – the -ς (-s) ending of μιλάς (milas) already says it. Greek drops words like 'I' and 'you' unless emphasizing.
No 'a' before jobs in Greek: είμαι δάσκαλος (ime dhaskalos) is literally 'I am teacher'. Same with any profession.
Many job words have a feminine form: δασκάλα (dhaskala) for a woman, δάσκαλος (dhaskalos) for a man.
Adjectives match the speaker: a man says κουρασμένος (kurasmenos), a woman κουρασμένη (kurasmeni).
With neuter nouns the adjective usually ends in -ο (-o): το παιδί είναι άρρωστο (to pedhi ine arosto).
Plural adjectives mark the group's gender: χαρούμενοι (kharumeni) for men or a mixed group, χαρούμενες (kharumenes) for women only.
Δεν (dhen) right before the verb makes it negative: δεν είμαι (dhen ime) = I am not. No 'do' needed.
Εγώ (egho) is pure emphasis – είμαι (ime) alone already means 'I am'. Adding it sounds like 'I, for one'.
Θα (tha) turns the present into the future: θα είμαι (tha ime) = I will be. No ending changes here – just add θα (tha).
Greek uses the plain present for near plans: μιλάμε αύριο (milame avrio) is literally 'we talk tomorrow' – no 'will' needed.
Παρακαλώ (parakalo) means both 'please' and 'you're welcome' – it's the standard reply to ευχαριστώ (efkharisto).
Συγγνώμη (sighnomi) does double duty: 'sorry' for mistakes and 'excuse me' to get someone's attention.
Γεια σας (ya sas) works both coming and going – it's 'hello' and 'goodbye' alike, like Italian ciao.
Τα λέμε (ta leme) is literally 'we say them' – 'them' meaning the things you'll talk about. It's the everyday 'see you / talk soon'.
'A/one' changes with gender: έναν αδερφό (enan adherfo = a brother), μία αδερφή (mia adherfi = a sister), ένα παιδί (ena pedhi = a child).
That ; at the end of εσύ έχεις αδέρφια; (esi ekhis adherfia) is the Greek question mark – Greek uses the semicolon where English uses ?
Μου (mu = my) comes after the noun: η οικογένειά μου (i ikoyenia mu), literally 'the family my'.
Possessives come after the noun, and the article stays: ο μπαμπάς μου (o babas mu) is literally 'the dad my'.
